title: Funding Contract Staff with IDEA, Title I and Medicaid
metaTitle: Using IDEA, Title I and Medicaid Funds for Contract Staff
description: Which federal funds can pay for contracted special education, related services and support roles, with IDEA, Title I, Medicaid and procurement rules cited.
answer: IDEA Part B, Title I, Title II, Title IV-A and school-based Medicaid can each pay for contracted school professionals when the service fits the fund's purpose. IDEA covers the excess cost of special education and related services under 34 CFR 300.202, with up to 15 percent usable for early intervening services. Each fund adds supplement, effort and procurement conditions.
keyTakeaways: IDEA Part B pays only the excess costs of special education and related services and must supplement, not supplant, other funds (34 CFR 300.202).
Up to 15 percent of a district's Part B allocation may fund coordinated early intervening services for K-12 students without IEPs (34 CFR 300.226).
Title I schoolwide and targeted programs may use nonprofit or for-profit external providers to deliver services (20 U.S.C. 6314(d) and 6315(h)).
Since CMS withdrew the free care policy on December 15, 2014, Medicaid can pay for covered school services regardless of charge, where the state plan allows (SMD #14-006).

Federally funded contracts follow 2 CFR 200.318 to 200.327: above your district's simplified acquisition threshold, which may not exceed the $350,000 FAR figure, formal competition and a cost or price analysis are required.
bodyHtml:
Which federal and state funds can pay for contracted school professionals?

Seven funding lines can carry contracted special education, related services and student support roles, each with its own condition. The sections after the table give the rule text and what your business office keeps on file.

FundWhat it may pay forContracted roles that commonly fitMain condition
IDEA Part B, section 611The excess costs of special education and related services for children with disabilities (34 CFR 300.202(a)(2)). Related services include speech-language pathology, psychological services, physical and occupational therapy, counseling, school nurse services and social work (34 CFR 300.34(a)).Special education teachers, paraprofessionals, SLPs, OTs, PTs, school psychologists, counselors, social workersExcess cost, supplement not supplant, local maintenance of effort (34 CFR 300.202 and 300.203)
IDEA Part B, section 619Special education and related services for children with disabilities aged 3 through 5 (20 U.S.C. 1419)Preschool special education teachers, SLPs, OTs, preschool paraprofessionalsSame Part B use-of-funds rules. For ages 3, 4 and 5, the excess cost rule does not bar paying all costs if no local or state funds serve nondisabled children of those ages (34 CFR 300.202(b)(1)(ii)).
Title I, Part ASchoolwide programs upgrade the whole school program; targeted programs serve the children with the greatest need (20 U.S.C. 6314 and 6315). Both allow services delivered by nonprofit or for-profit external providers (6314(d), 6315(h)).Intervention teachers, counselors, school-based mental health and specialized instructional support, tiered behavior supportSupplement not supplant, maintenance of effort and comparability (20 U.S.C. 6321). Schoolwide status needs 40 percent low-income or a state waiver.
Title II, Part ARecruiting, hiring and retaining effective teachers, including expert help screening candidates and enabling early hiring, and evidence-based class size reduction (20 U.S.C. 6613(b)(3)(B) and (D))Recruiting and screening support, teachers added for class size reductionSupplement not supplant (20 U.S.C. 6691). Activities may run through a contract with a for-profit or nonprofit entity (6613(a)(1)).
Title IV, Part ASafe and healthy students activities, including school-based mental health services and partnerships with businesses and nonprofits (20 U.S.C. 7118)School counselors, social workers, school psychologists, behavior supportAt least 20 percent to well-rounded education and 20 percent to safe and healthy students, unless the allocation is under $30,000 (20 U.S.C. 7116(e)(2), (f)). Supplement not supplant (7120).
School-based MedicaidReimbursement for Medicaid-covered services to Medicaid-enrolled students, under the approved state planSLPs, OTs, PTs, school psychologists, nurses, counselors, as your state plan defines covered providersThe furnishing provider must be enrolled; parental consent before first billing (34 CFR 300.154(d)(2)(iv)); no contingency-fee contracts in claimed costs
State special education aidSet by each state. Some states reimburse contracted services directly.Varies by state statuteState rules. State and local spending is what the IDEA maintenance of effort test counts (34 CFR 300.203(b)(2)).

Wisconsin is one example of state aid reaching contracted roles. Its Department of Public Instruction says private vendor contracts for substitute teachers, paraprofessionals, interpreters, educational audiology, speech therapy and several other services are eligible for state categorical aid and "may also be charged to the IDEA grant" (source: Wisconsin Department of Public Instruction, IDEA and state aid allowable costs).

What does IDEA Part B allow a district to pay for with contracted services?

IDEA Part B pays the excess costs of special education and related services for children with disabilities, and it must supplement state, local and other federal funds rather than replace them (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.202(a)). The rule is written about costs, not about who employs the provider, so a contracted SLP delivering IEP minutes sits inside the same cost category as one on your payroll. Four conditions decide whether a specific contract can be charged to the grant.

The excess cost requirement

Your district must spend at least a minimum average amount on the education of its children with disabilities before Part B funds are used (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.202(b)(2)(i)). Excess costs are the costs above the average annual per-student expenditure in the preceding school year, computed after deducting IDEA Part B, Title I Part A and Title III Part A amounts and the state or local funds spent on those programs. Capital outlay and debt service are excluded (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.16). Keep the calculation in the grant file.

Supplement not supplant and maintenance of effort

Each year your state agency checks that the district budgets at least as much for the education of children with disabilities as it spent in the most recent year with data, using one of four tests: local funds only, state and local funds combined, or either one per capita. At year end the district must show it did not spend less than the year before on at least one of those four tests, apart from the exceptions in 34 CFR 300.204 and 300.205 (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.203). If a district falls short, the state returns the shortfall or the district's Part B subgrant, whichever is lower, using non-federal funds (300.203(d)).

The practical risk: if an IDEA-funded contract replaces a provider your district paid with local funds last year, local special education spending can drop, and the test runs on that spending. Record which positions stay locally funded.

Coordinated early intervening services

A district may use up to 15 percent of its Part B allocation, less any amount it reduced local effort by under 34 CFR 300.205, for coordinated early intervening services for students in kindergarten through grade 12 who are not identified for special education but need extra academic and behavioral support, with particular emphasis on kindergarten through grade 3 (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.226(a)). Allowed activities include professional development and educational and behavioral evaluations, services and supports (300.226(b)).

Personnel qualifications apply to everyone delivering the service

The state sets qualifications for the personnel needed to carry out Part B. Related services personnel must meet state certification or licensing for their discipline and must not have had those requirements waived on an emergency, temporary or provisional basis. Paraprofessionals must be appropriately trained and supervised under state law (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.156(a) and (b)). A special education teacher needs full state certification as a special education teacher and at least a bachelor's degree (300.156(c)). Your contract file should hold the license verification for each person charged to the grant.

How does Medicaid reimbursement offset the cost of a contracted school SLP or other related service provider?

School-based Medicaid reimburses covered services delivered to Medicaid-enrolled students; it does not fund a position. CMS says Medicaid will pay for health-related services in an IEP if they are Medicaid-covered services, and that Medicaid is the payer of first resort for covered services in the IEP (source: CMS, Delivering Services in School-Based Settings: A Comprehensive Guide to Medicaid Services and Administrative Claiming, 2023).

The 2014 free care reversal

On December 15, 2014, CMS withdrew its earlier "free care" guidance in State Medicaid Director Letter #14-006. Under that letter, Medicaid reimbursement is available for covered services under the approved state plan "regardless of whether there is any charge for the service to the beneficiary or the community at large" (source: CMS, SMD #14-006). The 2023 guide adds that many state plans still tie school coverage to an IEP and would need an amendment to pay for services outside it. Your state plan decides.

Contracted providers can generate claims

A Medicaid-enrolled district can bill for services delivered by people on its payroll and by its contractors, or contract with Medicaid-enrolled providers who bill directly or are paid a contractual rate while the district claims the service. If the furnishing provider is not enrolled, Medicaid cannot pay. The same guide says Medicaid claims "may not include fees for contractor services that are based on, or include, contingency fee arrangements," and that contracts must follow federal procurement requirements. State plans differ on who qualifies, so confirm provider types with your state Medicaid agency before the contract is signed.

Parental consent and the no-cost rules

Before accessing a child's or parent's public benefits for the first time, the district must give written notice and obtain written parental consent that names the information disclosed, the purpose and the agency. Notice repeats every year. The district may not require Medicaid enrollment or pass on a co-pay, and still owes every required service if a parent refuses (source: eCFR, 34 CFR 300.154(d)(2)). The 2023 CMS guide notes the Department of Education proposed in May 2023 to change the consent rule; the consent requirement remains in the current eCFR text. Two more points matter for the budget: Medicaid proceeds are not program income, and Medicaid reimbursements spent on IDEA services do not count as state or local funds for maintenance of effort (300.154(g)). For the billing side, see our article on Medicaid billing for school-based therapy.

What procurement rules apply when federal money pays the contract?

When IDEA, Title I, Title II or Title IV money pays a staffing contract, the federal procurement standards in 2 CFR 200.318 through 200.327 apply. The Department of Education adopts 2 CFR part 200 for its grants (source: eCFR, 2 CFR 3474.1), and subrecipients such as school districts must follow 200.318 through 200.327 (source: eCFR, 2 CFR 200.317). Your written procurement procedures must also be consistent with state and local law (200.318(a)).

MethodWhen the rule allows itWhat to document
Micro-purchaseUp to the micro-purchase threshold. The FAR figure is $15,000; a district may self-certify up to $50,000 a year with a documented basis (2 CFR 200.320(a)(1)(iv)).That the price is reasonable, based on research, experience or purchase history
Simplified acquisitionAbove the micro-purchase threshold, up to the simplified acquisition threshold, which may not exceed the FAR figure of $350,000Price or rate quotations from an adequate number of qualified sources
Sealed bids or proposalsAbove your simplified acquisition threshold. Formal methods are competitive and require public notice.An independent estimate and a cost or price analysis (200.324(a)). For proposals, also the evaluation factors and their relative importance and written evaluation procedures (200.320(b)(2))
NoncompetitiveOnly in the five circumstances in 200.320(c)Which circumstance applies, and the facts behind it

The FAR figures are in 48 CFR 2.101 (source: eCFR, 48 CFR 2.101). Your district may set lower thresholds (source: eCFR, 2 CFR 200.320).

When the rule permits noncompetitive procurement

Section 200.320(c) lists five circumstances: the purchase is at or under the micro-purchase threshold; only a single source can fulfill it; a public exigency or emergency will not permit the delay of public notice; the federal agency or pass-through entity approves a written request; or competition is determined inadequate after soliciting several sources. Outside those five, the purchase is competed.

Rules that shape a staffing contract in particular

  • Hourly contracts. A contract priced as direct labor hours at fixed hourly rates is a time-and-materials contract. It may be used only after a determination that no other contract type is suitable, and it must set a ceiling price the contractor exceeds at its own risk (source: eCFR, 2 CFR 200.318(j)). Put a not-to-exceed amount in the board item.
  • Procurement records. The file must show the rationale for the method, the contract type, the selection or rejection of contractors and the basis for the price (200.318(i)).
  • Cooperative purchasing. Districts are encouraged to use intergovernmental and inter-entity agreements for common services, and documented procurement actions of this type meet the competition requirements of the part (200.318(e)). Our guide to cooperative purchasing for K-12 staffing covers how districts use it.
  • Reasonable cost. A cost is reasonable if a prudent person would incur it, considering market prices for comparable services in the geographic area (2 CFR 200.404(c)). For professional services, 200.459(b) adds factors including the necessity of contracting given the district's own capability and the adequacy of the agreement: description of service, time, rate and termination terms.
  • Checks before award. Confirm the vendor is not suspended or debarred (2 CFR 200.214), apply your conflict-of-interest standards, which cover board members (200.318(c)), and keep the records for 3 years after the final financial report (200.334).

If you are scoring vendors on a formal solicitation, our page on education staffing RFP experience sets out the documents to ask every bidder for.

What does a school board need to see before approving the contract?

A board needs one agenda item that answers five questions: what need, which roles for how long, which fund under which rule, which procurement method, and how results come back. Each answer points to a document already in the file.

  1. The need and the students affected. Open seats, IEP minutes at risk, caseloads. Our guide on the cost of an unfilled classroom lays out the cost lines a vacancy carries.
  2. The roles and the term. Role titles, licensure required under 34 CFR 300.156, start and end dates, not-to-exceed amount.
  3. The funding source and the rule that allows it. Fund, budget line, section number, and the supplement or excess cost test.
  4. Procurement method and documentation. Method under 2 CFR 200.320, price analysis, debarment check, conflict-of-interest statement.
  5. How results will be reported. Fill dates, IEP minutes delivered, Medicaid claims filed, conversions to district hires.

Sample justification language, with your facts in the brackets:

"The Office of Special Education requests approval of a contract with [vendor], selected by [procurement method] under Board Policy [number] and 2 CFR 200.320, for [number] [licensed role] from [start date] to [end date], not to exceed $[amount]. The services are required by the IEPs of [number] students and will be charged to IDEA Part B section 611 funds as excess costs under 34 CFR 300.202. Locally funded special education positions budgeted for this year remain funded, consistent with 34 CFR 300.203. Each provider will hold [state] licensure as required by 34 CFR 300.156. Where parents have consented under 34 CFR 300.154(d), covered services will be billed to Medicaid under the state plan and reported to the Board. Under the contract's temp-to-perm term, the district may hire a placed professional permanently at no conversion cost."

If the board is weighing contracts against a shrinking budget, our piece on staffing after the ESSER funding cliff covers the planning side.

faqs.q: Can IDEA Part B funds pay for a contracted speech-language pathologist?
faqs.a: Part B funds pay the excess costs of special education and related services, and speech-language pathology is a named related service in 34 CFR 300.34(a). The rule addresses the cost, not who employs the provider. The district must meet the excess cost and supplement not supplant tests in 34 CFR 300.202, keep local effort under 300.203, and confirm the provider meets state licensing under 300.156.

faqs.q: Can a district get Medicaid reimbursement for a contracted school SLP?
faqs.a: Yes, when the speech-language services are Medicaid-covered under your state plan, the student is Medicaid-enrolled, the parent has given the consent required by 34 CFR 300.154(d)(2)(iv), and the furnishing SLP is enrolled with Medicaid where your state requires it. The district can bill as the enrolled provider for its contractors, or the contracted provider can bill directly. If the furnishing provider is not enrolled, Medicaid cannot pay (CMS, 2023 school-based services guide).

faqs.q: Can Title I pay for services written into a student's IEP?
faqs.a: In a targeted assistance program, no. Under 20 U.S.C. 6315(c)(3), Title I funds may not provide services that are otherwise required by law for eligible children, including children with disabilities, but may coordinate or supplement those services. IDEA and state and local funds carry IEP services. Schoolwide programs follow different consolidation rules under 6314, so ask your state Title I office how your plan treats them.

faqs.q: Is an hourly staffing contract a time-and-materials contract under federal rules?
faqs.a: If the price is direct labor hours at fixed hourly rates covering wages, overhead and profit, it meets the definition in 2 CFR 200.318(j). The district may use that type only after determining that no other contract type is suitable, and the contract must carry a ceiling price the contractor exceeds at its own risk. A not-to-exceed amount in the board item records that ceiling.

faqs.q: What is the micro-purchase threshold for a district spending IDEA or Title I funds?
faqs.a: The base figure is the FAR micro-purchase threshold, listed as $15,000 in 48 CFR 2.101. Under 2 CFR 200.320(a)(1)(iv), a district may self-certify a higher threshold up to $50,000 each year if it documents a low-risk audit, an annual risk assessment or, for public institutions, consistency with state law. State and local law may set a lower threshold.

faqs.q: Does Medicaid reimbursement count toward IDEA maintenance of effort?
faqs.a: No. Under 34 CFR 300.154(g)(2), when a public agency spends reimbursements from federal funds such as Medicaid on IDEA services, those funds are not considered state or local funds for the maintenance of effort tests in 300.163 and 300.203. The same section says Medicaid proceeds are not program income under 2 CFR 200.307. Track Medicaid revenue separately from local special education spending.

faqs.q: Does a district need parental consent before billing Medicaid for IEP services?
faqs.a: Yes, under the current text of 34 CFR 300.154(d)(2)(iv). Before accessing a child's or parent's public benefits for the first time, the district must give written notice and obtain written consent naming the information to be disclosed, the purpose and the agency. Notice repeats annually. A parent's refusal does not relieve the district of providing every required service at no cost.

faqs.q: When may a district award a staffing contract without competition?
faqs.a: Only in the five circumstances in 2 CFR 200.320(c): the purchase is within the micro-purchase threshold, only a single source can fulfill it, a public exigency or emergency will not permit the delay of public notice, the federal agency or pass-through entity approves a written request, or competition is determined inadequate after soliciting several sources. The procurement file must record which one applies.
